front: Distinguish between "horizontal strabismus" and "torsional strabismus" regarding the specific muscle groups typically involved.
back:
• Horizontal: Medial and lateral recti
• Torsional: Superior and inferior obliques
• Vertical: Superior and inferior recti

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: Identify the primary clinical term for the condition where a child's eyes alternate in fixing on an object rather than using one dominant eye.
back:
• Alternating Strabismus
• Prevents permanent repression of one eye
• Maintains better bilateral acuity than dominant patterns

category: Illustrate the abnormalities of field of vision
front: A physiological blind spot occurs in the field of vision about 15 degrees lateral to the central point of vision due to the absence of rods and cones at the [___].
back:
* Optic disc
* Site where optic nerve fibers exit the eyeball
* Lack of photoreceptors prevents light detection

category: Illustrate the abnormalities of field of vision
front: A 45-year-old male with a pituitary adenoma presents with loss of vision in the lateral halves of both visual fields. Identify the specific site of the lesion.
back:
* Optic Chiasm
* Compression of decussating nasal retinal fibers
* Resultant Bitemporal Hemianopsia

category: Illustrate the abnormalities of field of vision
front: Explain the physiological basis of 'Macular Sparing' in a patient with a primary visual cortex stroke.
back:
* Dual blood supply to occipital pole (PCA and MCA)
* Massive cortical representation of the fovea
* Resists complete loss of central vision

category: Illustrate the abnormalities of field of vision
front: Contrast the visual field defects resulting from a lesion in the Temporal lobe (Meyer’s loop) versus the Parietal lobe.
back:
* Temporal: Superior homonymous quadrantanopsia ('Pie in the sky')
* Parietal: Inferior homonymous quadrantanopsia ('Pie on the floor')

category: Illustrate the abnormalities of field of vision
front: Describe the visual field abnormality produced by a complete transection of the Left Optic Tract.
back:
* Right Homonymous Hemianopsia
* Loss of the right temporal field and left nasal field
* Contralateral to the lesion site

category: Illustrate the abnormalities of field of vision
front: The clinical procedure used to chart the field of vision and detect abnormalities like scotomata is known as [___].
back:
* Perimetry
* Maps the extent of nasal and temporal vision
* Identifies location and size of blind spots

category: Illustrate the abnormalities of field of vision
front: A patient presents with progressive loss of peripheral vision, eventually leaving only a central 'tunnel' of sight. Identify this condition and its hallmark retinal finding.
back:
* Retinitis Pigmentosa
* Degeneration of peripheral rods
* Excessive melanin pigment deposition in degenerated areas

category: Illustrate the abnormalities of field of vision
front: Detail how pathologically high intraocular pressure in glaucoma leads to the formation of a scotoma.
back:
* Compression of optic nerve axons at the optic disc
* Blockage of axonal cytoplasmic flow
* Nutritional deficit leading to nerve fiber death

category: Illustrate the abnormalities of field of vision
front: Distinguish between the 'nasal field of vision' and the 'temporal field of vision' mapping relative to the retinal anatomy.
back:
* Nasal Field: Projected onto the temporal retina
* Temporal Field: Projected onto the nasal retina
* Temporal fibers remain ipsilateral; nasal fibers decussate

category: Illustrate the abnormalities of field of vision
front: Define a 'scotoma' and list two common toxic causes associated with this pathological blind spot.
back:
* Pathological blind spot in the visual field
* Causes: Lead poisoning or excessive tobacco use
* Also caused by allergic reactions in retina

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: The clinical condition characterized by the lack of fusion of the eyes in one or more visual coordinates is termed [___].
back:
• Strabismus (also known as squint or cross-eye)
• It involves a failure of the eyes to align on the same point
• Affects the horizontal, vertical, or rotational axes.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: A 4-year-old child presents with a permanent inward deviation of the right eye. The physician explains that the neuronal control pathways have an abnormal 'set'. Identify the three primary types of strabismus based on direction.
back:
• Horizontal strabismus
• Vertical strabismus
• Torsional (rotational) strabismus

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: Explain how the visual cortex functions as a controller to prevent strabismus in a normal individual.
back:
• It identifies when images from both eyes are 'out of register'
• It detects interference excitation in specific cortical neurons
• It sends motor signals to oculomotor muscles to adjust alignment.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: A patient with newly acquired paralysis of the superior oblique muscle exhibits a rotational misalignment. Identify the specific type of strabismus and the likely visual consequence.
back:
• Torsional strabismus
• Results in diplopia (double vision) because the brain cannot fuse the rotated image with the normal eye's image.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: Specify the primary neurological reason why visual acuity in a repressed eye may remain as low as 20/400 in adults with untreated childhood strabismus.
back:
• Failure to develop central synaptic connections
• Anatomical diminution of neuronal connections in the visual cortex
• Permanent sensory repression by the brain during critical development.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: In the classification of ocular misalignments, a [___] strabismus refers specifically to the lack of fusion in the up-and-down coordinate.
back:
• Vertical Strabismus
• It occurs when one eye is higher or lower than the other
• Often involves the superior or inferior rectus muscles.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: A child is diagnosed with strabismus where the eyes alternate in fixing on the object. Contrast the visual acuity prognosis of this child with one who only uses a single dominant eye.
back:
• Alternating fixation: Acuity develops relatively normally in both eyes
• Single eye fixation: The non-used eye becomes 'repressed', leading to permanent acuity loss.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: Describe the physiological 'set' that leads to the persistence of strabismus even after the initial muscular cause might be addressed.
back:
• The neuronal control pathways in the brain stem become 'set' in abnormal patterns
• Conjugate eye movement patterns are reinforced incorrectly
• This prevents the eyes from ever fusing naturally without intervention.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: Distinguish between the muscular involvement typically seen in horizontal strabismus versus torsional strabismus.
back:
• Horizontal: Involves the medial and lateral recti (side-to-side)
• Torsional: Involves the oblique muscles (rotational alignment).

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: Enlist the three visual coordinates that must be in register to achieve perfect binocular fusion.
back:
1. Horizontal coordinate
2. Vertical coordinate
3. Rotational (Torsional) coordinate

category: Explain the tri color mechanism of color determination
front: The Young-Helmholtz theory of color vision is based on the [___] mechanism, which states that all color gradations are perceived via the mixing of three primary monochromatic lights.
back:
• Tricolor (Trichromatic) mechanism.
• Utilizes three distinct types of cones.
• Based on red, green, and blue sensitivities.

category: Explain the tri color mechanism of color determination
front: A male patient is unable to distinguish red from green. Examination reveals he lacks red-sensitive cones entirely. Identify his specific clinical classification and the resulting change in his visual spectrum.
back:
• Protanope (Protanopia).
• Visual spectrum is noticeably shortened at the long-wavelength (red) end.
• X-linked recessive genetic disorder.

category: Explain the tri color mechanism of color determination
front: Explain the role of 'stimulation ratios' in the nervous system's interpretation of monochromatic orange light (580 nm).
back:
• Interpreted based on relative cone activation.
• Stimulates red cones (99%) and green cones (42%).
• Blue cones are not stimulated (ratio 99:42:0).

category: Explain the tri color mechanism of color determination
front: Two patients exhibit red-green color blindness. Patient A shows a shortened visual spectrum at the long-wavelength end, while Patient B has a normal spectral width. Contrast their underlying defects.
back:
• Patient A: Protanope (lacks red cones).
• Patient B: Deuteranope (lacks green cones).
• Red cones in Deuteranopes still detect long wavelengths, maintaining spectral width.

category: Explain the tri color mechanism of color determination
front: Describe the physiological requirements for the perception of 'White' light according to the tricolor mechanism.
back:
• Approximately equal stimulation of red, green, and blue cones.
• No single wavelength corresponds to white.
• It is a combination of all spectral wavelengths.

category: Explain the tri color mechanism of color determination
front: While the 11-cis retinal portion is identical in all visual pigments, the specific protein that determines the spectral sensitivity of a cone is called [___].
back:
• Photopsin (Cone Opsin).
• Three types exist (Blue, Green, Red).
• Combines with retinal to form color pigments.

category: Explain the tri color mechanism of color determination
front: A 10-year-old boy reads '21' on an Ishihara chart where the normal response is '74.' Explain the inheritance pattern and carrier status typical of this condition.
back:
• X-linked recessive inheritance.
• Passed from mother (carrier) to son.
• Approximately 8% of women are carriers.

category: Explain the tri color mechanism of color determination
front: Explain how peak absorbance wavelengths (445 nm, 535 nm, and 570 nm) facilitate the differentiation of the visual spectrum.
back:
• 445 nm: Peak for Blue cones.
• 535 nm: Peak for Green cones.
• 570 nm: Peak for Red cones.
• Overlapping curves allow unique stimulation ratios for every color.

category: Explain the tri color mechanism of color determination
front: Contrast the functionality of the 'opponent-color' ganglion cells with the tricolor mechanism of the cones.
back:
• Tricolor mechanism: Initial detection via three cone types.
• Opponent-color: Ganglion cells excited by one color but inhibited by another.
• Example: Red-excitation vs. Green-inhibition (or vice versa).

category: Explain the tri color mechanism of color determination
front: Identify the rare clinical condition involving the underrepresentation or absence of S-cones (short-wavelength sensitive).
back:
• Blue weakness (Tritanopia).
• Genetically inherited but extremely rare.
• Affects the blue-sensitive portion of the tricolor mechanism.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: The clinical condition characterized by a lack of fusion between the eyes in one or more visual coordinates is termed [___].
back:
- Strabismus (also known as squint or cross-eye).
- Results from the failure of both eyes to fixate simultaneously on an object.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: A 4-year-old child presents with a non-parallel gaze. Explain why this misalignment becomes permanent if the neuronal control pathways remain untreated.
back:
- The patterns of conjugate movements become abnormally 'set'.
- Neuronal control pathways in the brain fixate the eyes in a non-fused position.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: Describe how the visual cortex identifies a lack of register between the two eyes to initiate corrective ocular movements.
back:
- Cortical neurons experience 'interference excitation' when images are not fused.
- This triggers the oculomotor apparatus to adjust convergence, divergence, or rotation.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: Contrast horizontal, vertical, and torsional strabismus based on the axis of ocular misalignment.
back:
- Horizontal: Deviation in the medial-lateral plane.
- Vertical: Deviation in the upward-downward plane.
- Torsional: Rotational misalignment around the anteroposterior axis.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: Explain the anatomical consequence in the visual cortex when one eye is consistently repressed due to chronic strabismus.
back:
- Significant reduction in the number of neuronal connections from the repressed eye.
- Leads to permanent loss of visual acuity (amblyopia) in that eye.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: In the basic classification of strabismus, a misalignment occurring specifically in the rotational coordinate is called [___] strabismus.
back:
- Torsional strabismus.
- Often occurs in combination with horizontal or vertical deviations.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: A child with strabismus is observed to alternate fixation between both eyes. Apply this finding to predict the likely visual acuity outcome for both eyes.
back:
- Both eyes usually develop relatively normal visual acuity.
- This differs from 'repressed eye' cases where one eye becomes functionally blind.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: How does the 'interference' neuron activity in the visual cortex respond once the eyes successfully bring corresponding retinal points into register?
back:
- The specific excitation of interference neurons disappears.
- This signals the oculomotor system that the eyes are correctly fused.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: Distinguish between the two primary ways a child’s central nervous system adapts to the double vision (diplopia) of strabismus.
back:
- Alternating Fixation: Using each eye sequentially.
- Suppression: Permanently ignoring the signal from the non-dominant, repressed eye.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: Enlist the three basic types of strabismus based on the visual coordinates provided in clinical physiology.
back:
1. Horizontal strabismus.
2. Vertical strabismus.
3. Torsional strabismus.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: Strabismus, commonly referred to as "squint" or "cross-eye," is physiologically defined as the lack of [___] of the eyes in one or more visual coordinates.
back:
- Fusion
- Failure of the eyes to align on corresponding retinal points
- Results in a lack of binocular "register."

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: A 4-year-old boy's right eye persistently deviates medially while his left eye fixates on a target. Identify the likely classification of this strabismus based on the plane of deviation.
back:
- Horizontal Strabismus
- Specifically Esotropia (inward deviation)
- Most common directional type.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: Explain the role of the cortical "interference" signal in the normal prevention of strabismus.
back:
- Visual cortex neurons detect when images are not "in register."
- Disparity causes interference excitation.
- Triggers oculomotor signals to converge, diverge, or rotate eyes until fusion occurs.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: A patient presents with an eye that rotates abnormally around its anteroposterior axis. Contrast this 'Torsional Strabismus' with 'Vertical Strabismus' regarding the primary axis of displacement.
back:
- Torsional: Rotational displacement around the visual axis.
- Vertical: Upward or downward displacement.
- Both prevent proper binocular fusion.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: Enlist the three primary visual coordinates in which fusion may be lacking in a patient with a 'squint'.
back:
1. Horizontal
2. Vertical
3. Torsional (Rotational)

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: In a child with constant unilateral strabismus, the brain may permanently ignore signals from the deviating eye, a process known as [___].
back:
- Suppression (or Repression)
- Leads to Amblyopia (lazy eye)
- Visual acuity often drops to 20/400 or less.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: A young child fixates on objects using either eye alternately but never both simultaneously. Predict the likely outcome for his central nervous system synaptic connections if left untreated.
back:
- Synaptic connections from the repressed eye diminish in the visual cortex.
- Lack of stereopsis (depth perception).
- Permanent deficit in visual acuity if not corrected during the plastic period.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: Describe the physiological 'Set' mechanism and how its abnormality leads to the development of congenital strabismus.
back:
- Fusion mechanism must be 'set' in early childhood.
- Abnormal 'set' occurs when one eye fails to fixate simultaneously with the other.
- Neuronal control pathways eventually lock into this abnormal conjugate movement pattern.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: Distinguish between 'Alternating' and 'Unilateral' strabismus regarding the risk of developing permanent amblyopia.
back:
- Alternating: Eyes take turns fixating; visual acuity develops relatively well in both.
- Unilateral: One eye is always repressed; high risk of severe, permanent blindness in that eye.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: Name the specialized visual perception capability that is typically lost in all types of strabismus due to lack of retinal register.
back:
- Stereopsis
- Also known as depth perception
- Requires fusion of slightly disparate images from both retinas.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: Strabismus, commonly referred to as squint or cross-eye, is clinically defined as the lack of [___] of the eyes in one or more of the visual coordinates.
back:
• Fusion
• It represents a failure of both eyes to align on the same point of interest simultaneously across horizontal, vertical, or torsional planes.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: A 4-year-old child's right eye consistently deviates toward the nasal bridge while the left eye fixates on a target. Identify this specific horizontal strabismus.
back:
• Esotropia
• This is a type of horizontal strabismus characterized by inward deviation of the visual axis.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: Explain the underlying developmental etiology of strabismus in early childhood regarding conjugate movement patterns.
back:
• Abnormal 'set' of the fusion mechanism during initial efforts to fixate.
• Conjugate movement patterns become incorrectly programmed in neuronal control pathways, preventing simultaneous alignment.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: Contrast 'Exotropia' with 'Esotropia' regarding the direction of horizontal ocular misalignment.
back:
• Exotropia: Outward (lateral) deviation of the visual axis.
• Esotropia: Inward (nasal) deviation of the visual axis.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: Enlist the three primary visual coordinates in which lack of fusion may manifest as strabismus.
back:
• Horizontal coordinate
• Vertical coordinate
• Torsional (rotational) coordinate

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: In vertical strabismus, a downward deviation of the visual axis is termed [___].
back:
• Hypotropia
• This occurs when one eye is misaligned inferiorly relative to the fixating eye.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: A pediatric patient demonstrates a rotational misalignment where the eyeball rotates around its anteroposterior axis. Identify the classification of this strabismus.
back:
• Torsional strabismus
• This involves abnormal rotational positioning, often linked to superior or inferior oblique muscle dysfunction.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: Describe the role of the Superior Colliculi in the involuntary locking mechanism that prevents strabismus in healthy individuals.
back:
• Provides topographic mapping of the retina.
• Triggers sudden 'flicking' movements (saccades) to return an image to the fovea if it drifts, maintaining fusion.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: Distinguish between 'Hypertropia' and 'Hypotropia' within the vertical coordinate of strabismus.
back:
• Hypertropia: Upward deviation of the visual axis.
• Hypotropia: Downward deviation of the visual axis.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: Mention the primary anatomical consequence for the visual cortex when strabismus results in a chronically repressed eye during childhood.
back:
• Diminished neuronal connections
• Cortical areas that should receive signals from the repressed eye fail to develop, leading to permanent low visual acuity (Amblyopia).

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: Strabismus, also clinically known as squint or cross-eye, is defined as a lack of [___] between the two eyes in one or more visual coordinates.
back:
• Fusion
• It involves the inability of the visual axes to remain in register
• Prevents the coordination of images from both retinas into a single perception.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: A 5-year-old child presents with an eye that persistently deviates inward toward the nose. Identify the specific category of strabismus and the likely long-term cortical consequence if untreated.
back:
• Horizontal Strabismus (Esotropia)
• Suppression/Amblyopia: The brain represses the image from the deviating eye to avoid diplopia
• Results in permanent loss of visual acuity in the repressed eye.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: Explain the physiological basis of the 'abnormal set' theory in the development of childhood strabismus.
back:
• Initial failure to fixate both eyes on the same object
• Abnormal 'setting' of neuronal conjugate movement pathways
• Causes permanent lack of fusion despite anatomically normal extraocular muscles.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: Contrast the visual outcome of strabismus that alternates between eyes with strabismus where one eye is exclusively dominant.
back:
• Alternating: Both eyes develop relatively normal acuity as they take turns fixing
• One-eye Dominant: The repressed eye develops severe vision loss (20/400) due to diminished cortical synaptic connections.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: Enlist the three primary visual coordinates in which fusion may be lost in various types of strabismus.
back:
• Horizontal (Inward or Outward deviation)
• Vertical (Upward or Downward deviation)
• Torsional (Rotational deviation)

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: In patients with strabismus, the loss of the neural mechanism for [___] prevents the accurate judgment of distances for nearby objects.
back:
• Stereopsis (or Depth Perception)
• Occurs because corresponding points on the two retinas are no longer in register
• Prevents the brain from calculating image disparity.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: An adult patient who has had a repressed eye since childhood due to strabismus loses their dominant eye in an accident. Describe the prognosis for visual recovery in the previously repressed eye.
back:
• Poor prognosis: Acuity usually remains at 20/400
• Visual development is highly dependent on early childhood synaptic development
• Adult cortical connections rarely recover once diminished.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: Describe how the visual cortex attempts to correct 'non-register' of images before strabismus becomes permanent.
back:
• Interaction between cortical neurons causes interference excitation
• Signals the oculomotor apparatus to adjust directional gaze
• Triggers convergence, divergence, or rotation to re-establish fusion.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: Distinguish between the roles of 'Voluntary' and 'Involuntary' fixation areas in maintaining ocular alignment.
back:
• Voluntary (Frontal Lobe): Moves eyes to find the object of interest
• Involuntary (Occipital Cortex): Locks the fovea on the object via negative feedback
• Strabismus often involves the 'locking' mechanism failing.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: Name the brain stem structure primarily responsible for the 'flicking' movements that prevent an image from drifting off the fovea during fixation.
back:
• Superior Colliculus
• Coordinates the involuntary locking mechanism
• Responsible for topographical mapping of the retina to control oculomotor nuclei.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: Strabismus is defined as the lack of fusion of the eyes in one or more visual coordinates, resulting from an abnormal 'set' of the [___] mechanism in the visual system.
back:
• Fusion
• This mechanism normally aligns the eyes so corresponding retinal points are in register
• Failure leads to misalignment in horizontal, vertical, or torsional planes.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: A 5-year-old child presents with a persistent inward deviation of the left eye. This specific subtype of horizontal strabismus is clinically termed [___].
back:
• Esotropia
• It is a form of horizontal strabismus
• If untreated, the brain may repress the visual image from the deviated eye to avoid double vision.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: Explain how the visual cortex normally prevents strabismus through the use of 'interference' neurons.
back:
• Cortical neurons detect when images are not 'in register'
• Non-fusion causes interference excitation
• This sends corrective motor signals to oculomotor muscles to adjust convergence or rotation.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: Contrast the visual outcome in a child who alternates fixation between both eyes versus a child who only uses the dominant eye due to strabismus.
back:
• Alternating fixation: Visual acuity develops normally in both eyes
• Single-eye dominance: The non-dominant eye becomes 'repressed'
• Result: Permanent reduction in synaptic connections and visual acuity (Amblyopia).

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: Enlist the three primary visual coordinates in which fusion may fail, leading to different classifications of strabismus.
back:
• Horizontal (Esotropia/Exotropia)
• Vertical (Hypertropia/Hypotropia)
• Torsional (Cyclotropia)
• Combinations of these three coordinates often occur simultaneously.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: In the context of pediatric ophthalmology, 'cross-eye' or 'squint' resulting from a lack of binocular coordination is formally known as [___].
back:
• Strabismus
• It is characterized by the failure of the eyes to fixate on the same point simultaneously
• It often involves a faulty feedback loop in the superior colliculi.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: A patient presents with an eye that deviates outward (temporally). Identify this specific type of strabismus and the likely muscle imbalance involved.
back:
• Exotropia
• A subtype of horizontal strabismus
• Usually involves a relative overactivity of the lateral rectus or weakness of the medial rectus muscle.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: Describe the physiological basis of 'Torsional Strabismus' and which extraocular muscles are primarily responsible for this coordinate.
back:
• Failure to maintain the visual field in an upright position
• Involves rotational misalignment of the eyeball
• Primarily mediated by the superior and inferior oblique muscles.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: Distinguish between 'Hypertropia' and 'Hypotropia' within the classification of vertical strabismus.
back:
• Hypertropia: Upward deviation of the eye
• Hypotropia: Downward deviation of the eye
• Both represent a failure of fusion in the vertical coordinate plane.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: Identify the critical sensory deficit that occurs in all types of strabismus, limiting the patient's ability to judge distances.
back:
• Loss of Stereopsis (Binocular Depth Perception)
• Caused by the failure of images to fall on 'corresponding points' of the two retinas
• Affects distance judgment up to 200 feet.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: Strabismus, commonly referred to as squint, is defined as the lack of [___] of the eyes in one or more visual coordinates.
back:
* Fusion.
* It involves the failure of both eyes to align simultaneously on the same object of attention.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: A 5-year-old child is observed to have a permanent inward deviation of the left eye. Identify the specific sub-type of horizontal strabismus and the most likely cortical complication.
back:
* Esotropia.
* Amblyopia (lazy eye) due to chronic suppression of the visual image in the deviated eye.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: Explain why the 'set' of the fusion mechanism is critical in early childhood development to prevent strabismus.
back:
* The brain must learn to conjugate eye movements.
* Early failure to fixate both eyes leads to an abnormal neuronal 'set' in control pathways.
* Once 'set' incorrectly, the eyes may never achieve fusion.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: Contrast 'Exotropia' and 'Hypotropia' in terms of the direction of ocular deviation.
back:
* Exotropia: Horizontal strabismus where the eye deviates outward (laterally).
* Hypotropia: Vertical strabismus where the eye deviates downward.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: Identify the three primary visual coordinates in which fusion may be lost in a patient with squint.
back:
* Horizontal.
* Vertical.
* Rotational (Torsional).

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: In cases of monocular strabismus where one eye is repressed, the loss of visual acuity is primarily due to [___] rather than an organic defect of the eye itself.
back:
* Failure of central synaptic connections.
* The visual cortex loses connections from the repressed eye due to lack of use during development.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: A patient presents with an inability to keep the eyes aligned specifically when looking up or down. Name the category of strabismus and the muscles likely involved.
back:
* Vertical Strabismus.
* Superior and Inferior Recti muscles (or the Obliques).

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: Describe the physiological outcome if a child with strabismus alternates between fixing with the left and right eye instead of using only one.
back:
* Prevention of amblyopia.
* Visual acuity may develop normally in both eyes, though binocular stereopsis is still lost.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: Distinguish between 'Concomitant' and 'Non-concomitant' strabismus based on gaze direction.
back:
* Concomitant: Deviation remains constant in all directions of gaze.
* Non-concomitant: Angle of deviation changes depending on gaze direction (usually indicates paralytic origin).

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: Enlist the three basic classifications of strabismus based on the axis of ocular misalignment.
back:
* Horizontal Strabismus.
* Vertical Strabismus.
* Torsional Strabismus.

category: Illustrate the abnormalities of field of vision
front: The physiological blind spot, caused by the absence of photoreceptors over the optic disc, is located approximately [___] degrees lateral to the central point of vision.
back:
• 15 degrees
• Represents the exit point of the optic nerve
• Lacks both rods and cones

category: Illustrate the abnormalities of field of vision
front: A 50-year-old patient notes a progressive loss of peripheral vision, while central vision remains relatively intact. Fundoscopy reveals dark melanin deposits in the peripheral retina. Identify the condition.
back:
• Retinitis pigmentosa
• Degenerative disease of the retina
• Causes 'tunnel vision' before encroaching on the center

category: Illustrate the abnormalities of field of vision
front: Explain how pathologically high intraocular pressure in glaucoma leads to abnormalities in the field of vision.
back:
• Compresses optic nerve axons at the optic disc
• Blocks axonal flow of cytoplasm to the brain
• Reduces nutrition/blood supply (retinal artery compression)
• Leads to death of retinal fibers and scotomata

category: Illustrate the abnormalities of field of vision
front: Contrast the physiological blind spot with a pathological scotoma in terms of etiology and clinical significance.
back:
• Blind Spot: Normal anatomical feature due to optic disc anatomy
• Scotoma: Pathological blind spot indicating disease
• Scotoma causes: Glaucoma, lead poisoning, or tobacco toxicity

category: Illustrate the abnormalities of field of vision
front: Enumerate the three primary coordinates of vision where a lack of fusion (strabismus) can occur.
back:
• Horizontal (most common)
• Vertical
• Torsional (rotational)

category: Illustrate the abnormalities of field of vision
front: The clinical process used to chart the field of vision and diagnose specific blind spots in the retina is known as [___].
back:
• Perimetry
• Subject indicates when objects are seen/not seen
• Maps nasal and temporal field boundaries

category: Illustrate the abnormalities of field of vision
front: A patient presents with small, irregular pupils that do not constrict when exposed to bright light but do constrict when focusing on a near object. Name this diagnostic finding.
back:
• Argyll Robertson pupil
• Characteristic of CNS syphilis (neurosyphilis)
• Result of damage to the pretectal inhibitory pathways

category: Illustrate the abnormalities of field of vision
front: Describe the central nervous system's response to chronic lack of fusion in one eye during early childhood development.
back:
• Visual image from the misaligned eye is repressed
• Central synaptic connections from that eye diminish
• Results in low visual acuity (amblyopia) in the repressed eye

category: Illustrate the abnormalities of field of vision
front: Distinguish between the nasal and temporal fields of vision based on the retinal halves that perceive them.
back:
• Nasal field: Perceived by the temporal half of the retina
• Temporal field: Perceived by the nasal half of the retina
• Nasal retinal fibers cross at the chiasm

category: Illustrate the abnormalities of field of vision
front: Identify the three primary ocular/facial signs of Horner's Syndrome resulting from sympathetic interruption.
back:
• Miosis (constricted pupil)
• Ptosis (drooping eyelid due to smooth muscle paralysis)
• Anhidrosis (lack of sweating on the affected side)

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: Strabismus is defined as the lack of [___] of the eyes in one or more visual coordinates, including the horizontal, vertical, or rotational axes.
back:
• Fusion
• It occurs when the visual axes do not align on a single point of fixation.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: A 4-year-old child presents with a permanent inward deviation of the right eye relative to the left. Identify this specific subtype of horizontal strabismus.
back:
• Esotropia (Internal Strabismus)
• Often referred to as 'cross-eye'.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: Explain why visual acuity fails to develop in the non-fixing eye of a child with constant, unilateral strabismus.
back:
• Sensory repression by the brain to avoid diplopia
• Diminished neuronal synaptic connections in the visual cortex
• Leads to Amblyopia (lazy eye).

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: Contrast the misalignment planes in Torsional strabismus versus Vertical strabismus.
back:
• Torsional: Rotational misalignment around the visual axis
• Vertical: Upward (Hypertropia) or downward (Hypotropia) misalignment.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: Enlist the three primary visual coordinate planes used to classify the types of strabismus.
back:
• Horizontal
• Vertical
• Rotational (Torsional).

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: In the clinical assessment of a 'squint,' an outward deviation of the eye away from the midline is termed [___].
back:
• Exotropia
• A subtype of horizontal strabismus.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: A patient presents with 'Hypertropia' of the left eye. Describe the physical orientation of the visual axes in this condition.
back:
• The left visual axis is deviated upward
• Type: Vertical strabismus
• Result: Lack of fusion on the vertical coordinate.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: How does the 'abnormal set' of neuronal control pathways contribute to the progression of strabismus in early childhood?
back:
• Failure of initial fixation efforts prevents proper fusion
• Conjugate movement patterns become 'fixed' in the brainstem nuclei
• Leads to permanent inability to fuse images.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: Differentiate between the terms 'Esotropia' and 'Exotropia' regarding the direction of the visual axis deviation.
back:
• Esotropia: Inward (nasal) deviation
• Exotropia: Outward (temporal) deviation.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: Identify the specific brain region responsible for detecting 'interference' when images are not in register, thereby driving fusion movements.
back:
• Visual Cortex (Primary and Secondary areas)
• It triggers motor signals to oculomotor apparatus to restore register.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: Strabismus is physiologically characterized as a lack of [___] between the eyes in one or more of the visual coordinates.
back:
* Fusion
* Can affect horizontal, vertical, or rotational (torsional) axes.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: A patient with long-standing monocular strabismus suddenly loses vision in their dominant eye. Describe the expected outcome for the previously repressed eye.
back:
* Acuity develops only slightly in adults.
* Significant recovery is only possible in young children.
* Limited by permanent reduction in cortical synaptic connections.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: Explain the neural basis for the development of childhood strabismus according to the 'abnormal set' theory.
back:
* Failure of early efforts to fixate both eyes simultaneously.
* Patterns of conjugate eye movements become incorrectly 'set.'
* Results in permanent misalignment in neuronal control pathways.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: Contrast Horizontal Strabismus with Torsional Strabismus based on the axis of ocular misalignment.
back:
* Horizontal: Misalignment along the lateral-medial axis (esotropia/exotropia).
* Torsional: Rotational misalignment of the eyeballs.
* Both result from a failure of the fusion mechanism.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: List the three visual coordinates in which a lack of eye fusion can occur to define Strabismus.
back:
* Horizontal coordinate
* Vertical coordinate
* Rotational (Torsional) coordinate

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: In strabismus, when the brain ignores the visual signal from the non-fixing eye to prevent double vision, the process is termed [___] of the visual image.
back:
* Suppression
* Prevents diplopia.
* Leads to failure of visual acuity development in that eye.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: A child presents with eyes that take turns fixing on objects. Identify this pattern and its effect on long-term visual acuity compared to constant monocular deviation.
back:
* Alternating Strabismus.
* Benefit: Both eyes typically develop normal visual acuity.
* Contrast: Monocular deviation causes one eye to become 'repressed' and amblyopic.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: Explain how the visual cortex utilize 'interference excitation' to prevent the development of strabismus.
back:
* Interaction between cortical neurons detects if images are not 'in register.'
* Non-register triggers 'interference excitation.'
* This signal drives oculomotor muscles to adjust convergence/rotation for fusion.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: Distinguish between the primary muscles typically involved in Horizontal vs. Vertical Strabismus.
back:
* Horizontal: Medial and Lateral Recti.
* Vertical: Superior/Inferior Recti or the Oblique muscles.
* Misalignment stems from an imbalance in these antagonistic pairs.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: Enumerate the three basic types of strabismus based on the direction of eye deviation.
back:
* Horizontal strabismus
* Vertical strabismus
* Torsional strabismus

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: The condition characterized by the lack of fusion of the eyes in one or more visual coordinates, such as horizontal, vertical, or rotational, is termed [___].
back:
Strabismus (also known as squint or cross-eye).
- Represents a failure of the eyes to align on corresponding retinal points.
- Results in a lack of binocular vision/fusion.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: A 4-year-old child presents with a persistent inward deviation of the left eye. The ophthalmologist notes the visual axes are not in register along the X-axis. Identify the specific type of strabismus.
back:
Horizontal strabismus.
- Involves misalignment in the horizontal coordinate.
- Can present as esotropia (inward) or exotropia (outward) deviation.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: Explain the primary neurological cause of strabismus in young children during the development of gaze fixation.
back:
Abnormal "set" of the fusion mechanism:
- Early failure to fixate both eyes simultaneously on one object.
- Neuronal control pathways for conjugate movements become permanently misaligned/set.
- Prevents future simultaneous binocular fixation.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: Contrast the clinical outcome of strabismus in a patient who exhibits alternating fixation versus a patient who uses only one dominant eye.
back:
- Alternating Fixation: Both eyes develop relatively normal visual acuity as they are used interchangeably.
- Single Dominance: The unused eye is chronically repressed, leading to amblyopia and loss of cortical synaptic connections.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: Describe the secondary effect on the visual cortex when one eye in a strabismus patient is chronically repressed to avoid diplopia.
back:
- Reduced number of functional neuronal connections in specific cortical layers.
- Permanent reduction in visual acuity (e.g., 20/400).
- Only slightly reversible in adults if the dominant eye is lost.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: Strabismus involving the rotation of the eyeballs around the visual axis, preventing the maintenance of an upright visual field, is classified as [___] strabismus.
back:
Torsional strabismus.
- Involves rotational misalignment of the globe.
- Often associated with dysfunction of the superior or inferior oblique muscles.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: A patient presents with a visual axis misalignment where one eye is significantly higher than the other. Name this type of strabismus and the coordinate involved.
back:
Vertical strabismus.
- Misalignment occurs in the vertical coordinate.
- Involves the superior rectus, inferior rectus, or oblique muscle groups.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: In a patient with non-fused eyes, describe the sensory mechanism utilized by the brain to prevent the perception of two different images (diplopia).
back:
Sensory Suppression:
- The brain actively inhibits the visual signal from the non-fixing eye.
- Prevents double vision by ignoring the repressed image.
- Leads to developmental amblyopia in children.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: Distinguish between the roles of the Frontal and Occipital eye fields in the context of strabismus management.
back:
- Frontal Fields (Voluntary): Essential to "unlock" gaze from one target to find another.
- Occipital Fields (Involuntary): Responsible for the negative feedback "locking" mechanism that maintains binocular fusion.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: Enlist the three primary types of strabismus based on the coordinate of visual misalignment.
back:
1. Horizontal strabismus.
2. Vertical strabismus.
3. Torsional strabismus.
- Note: Patients often present with combinations of two or all three types.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: The clinical condition defined as a lack of fusion of the eyes in one or more visual coordinates is termed [___].
back:
● Strabismus (or Squint)
● Results in misalignment of the visual axes
● Prevents the images from falling on corresponding retinal points

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: A 4-year-old child presents with an eye that consistently turns inward while the other fixates. If left untreated, the brain may permanently suppress the misaligned image to prevent diplopia, leading to [___].
back:
● Amblyopia (Lazy Eye)
● Occurs due to the repression of the non-fixating eye
● Causes a developmental failure of visual acuity in the repressed eye

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: Explain the neural mechanism leading to the development of 'set' conjugate movement abnormalities in childhood strabismus.
back:
● Early failure to fixate both eyes on one object
● Abnormal patterns become 'set' in neuronal control pathways
● Leads to permanent loss of the fusion mechanism

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: Contrast the primary features of horizontal strabismus with those of torsional strabismus.
back:
● Horizontal: Involves medial (esotropia) or lateral (exotropia) deviation
● Torsional: Involves rotation of the eyeballs around the visual axis
● Horizontal affects side-to-side alignment; Torsional affects visual field uprightness

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: Identify the three primary visual coordinates in which fusion may be lost in strabismus.
back:
● Horizontal coordinate
● Vertical coordinate
● Rotational (Torsional) coordinate
● Note: Combinations of all three types frequently occur

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: The specific type of strabismus where one eye deviates upward or downward relative to the other is classified as [___] strabismus.
back:
● Vertical strabismus
● Result of imbalance in the superior or inferior recti
● Prevents vertical alignment of the two visual fields

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: An adult patient presents with sudden-onset ocular misalignment and complains of seeing two of every object. Why does this patient experience diplopia while a young child with the same condition does not?
back:
● Adults have fully developed visual cortex synapses
● They cannot easily suppress/repress the second image
● Children exhibit cortical plasticity, allowing for suppression of the misaligned image

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: How does the visual outcome of 'alternating strabismus' differ from that of constant uniocular strabismus?
back:
● Alternating: Eyes take turns fixating; both maintain connections to the cortex
● Uniocular: One eye is permanently repressed; leads to severe loss of acuity (amblyopia)
● Alternating prevents the permanent blinding of one eye

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: Contrast the involvement of the recti muscles versus the oblique muscles in horizontal and torsional strabismus.
back:
● Horizontal: Primarily involves the medial and lateral recti muscles
● Torsional: Primarily involves the superior and inferior oblique muscles
● Vertical: Primarily involves the superior and inferior recti

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: State the anatomical change observed in the primary visual cortex of a patient with chronic, untreated uniocular strabismus.
back:
● Diminished number of neuronal connections
● Affects specific cortical areas assigned to the repressed eye
● Result of chronic lack of sensory input stimulation

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: Strabismus is physiologically defined as a lack of [___] between the two eyes in one or more of the visual coordinates.
back:
Fusion
- Occurs in horizontal, vertical, or torsional coordinates.
- Results in the eyes failing to align on the same point of interest simultaneously.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: A 4-year-old child presents with a 'squint' where only one eye fixates on a target at a time. The brain's compensatory mechanism to prevent diplopia in this patient is [___].
back:
Sensory Suppression (Repression)
- The brain ignores the signal from the non-fixing eye.
- Prevents double vision but leads to decreased visual acuity (amblyopia) in that eye.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: Explain the underlying developmental cause of strabismus related to the 'neuronal set' of the conjugate movement system.
back:
Neuronal Set Abnormality
- Early failure to fixate both eyes leads to abnormal patterns in control pathways.
- These conjugate movements become 'set' in the brainstem, preventing future fusion.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: Contrast the clinical presentation of 'alternating' strabismus with 'monocular' (repressed) strabismus.
back:
Alternating vs Monocular:
- Alternating: Eyes take turns fixing; visual acuity is usually preserved in both.
- Monocular: One eye is never used; leads to permanent suppression and 20/400 vision (amblyopia).

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: Enlist the three primary types of strabismus categorized by the spatial coordinate of the misalignment.
back:
Primary Types:
1. Horizontal Strabismus (most common)
2. Vertical Strabismus
3. Torsional Strabismus

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: The clinical condition resulting from chronic suppression of visual signals in a strabismic eye, characterized by a lack of proper synaptic development in the visual cortex, is [___].
back:
Amblyopia (Ex Anopsia)
- Often called 'lazy eye'.
- Acuity can be as low as 20/400.
- Irreversible in adults if not treated during the critical period of childhood.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: A patient is unable to perceive depth despite having clear vision in each eye separately. Identify the likely abnormality in binocular coordinate alignment.
back:
Strabismus (Lack of Fusion)
- Without fusion, stereopsis (depth perception) is impossible.
- The visual images cannot be brought into 'register' on corresponding retinal points.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: How do the three pairs of extraocular muscles relate to the three basic types of strabismus?
back:
Muscle-Type Relation:
- Medial/Lateral Recti: Horizontal Strabismus.
- Superior/Inferior Recti: Vertical Strabismus.
- Superior/Inferior Obliques: Torsional Strabismus.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: Distinguish between 'Squint' and 'Stereopsis' in terms of the cortical 'interference' excitation mechanism.
back:
Fusion vs Interference:
- Stereopsis: Disparate images are 'in register' via interference excitation in the cortex.
- Squint (Strabismus): Cortical neurons remain excited by 'non-register' signals, failing to establish fusion.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: Define the term 'Torsional Strabismus' in terms of eyeball rotation.
back:
Torsional Strabismus
- Misalignment involving the rotational coordinate of the eye.
- Typically involves dysfunction of the Superior or Inferior Oblique muscles.

category: Describe the muscular and neural control of eye movements
front: The [___] is the primary brainstem nerve tract responsible for the reciprocal innervation and coordination between the nuclei of the third, fourth, and sixth cranial nerves.
back:
• Medial Longitudinal Fasciculus (MLF)
• Interconnects brainstem nuclei for conjugate gaze
• Links vestibular nuclei to oculomotor apparatus for equilibrium control

category: Describe the muscular and neural control of eye movements
front: A patient presents with a persistent medially deviated eye and an inability to abduct the eyeball laterally. This presentation most likely indicates a palsy of the [___].
back:
• Abducens nerve (Cranial Nerve VI)
• Innervates the lateral rectus muscle
• Results in diplopia (double vision) and failure of lateral gaze

category: Describe the muscular and neural control of eye movements
front: Explain the role of the three types of continuous fixation movements (tremor, drift, and flick) in maintaining visual focus.
back:
• Tremor/Drift: Constant, imperceptible movements that shift images across foveal cones
• Flick: Triggered when an image reaches the foveal edge
• Reflexively moves the image back to the central point of vision

category: Describe the muscular and neural control of eye movements
front: Contrast the voluntary fixation area and the involuntary fixation area regarding their anatomical location and clinical significance of damage.
back:
• Voluntary: Located in frontal premotor cortex; damage makes 'unlocking' gaze difficult
• Involuntary: Located in secondary occipital cortex; damage prevents 'locking' onto an object
• Occipital fields prevent drift; frontal fields initiate the search for targets

category: Describe the muscular and neural control of eye movements
front: Explain the physiological significance of 'saccadic movements' during activities like reading or viewing a moving scene.
back:
• High-speed 'jumps' (2-3 per second) between highlights
• Brain suppresses the visual image during the jump
• Maximizes time (90%) spent on high-acuity fixation rather than blurred movement

category: Describe the muscular and neural control of eye movements
front: The [___] muscles function primarily to rotate the eyeballs to maintain the visual fields in a stable, upright position.
back:
• Oblique muscles (Superior and Inferior Obliques)
• Coordinate torsional movements
• Essential for stabilizing the image during head tilt

category: Describe the muscular and neural control of eye movements
front: A child with untreated strabismus (lack of fusion) is found to have significantly reduced visual acuity in one eye despite normal retinal health. Describe the cortical basis for this loss.
back:
• Amblyopia (Suppression)
• Visual cortex represses the non-fused image to avoid confusion
• Results in permanent loss of synaptic connections from the repressed eye if uncorrected

category: Describe the muscular and neural control of eye movements
front: Describe how the superior colliculi coordinate the 'global orientation reflex' in response to a sudden lateral visual or auditory stimulus.
back:
• Topographical mapping of M-fiber retinal inputs
• Integration of visual, acoustic, and somatic signals
• Transmission via MLF to nuclei for turning eyes, head, and the whole body

category: Describe the muscular and neural control of eye movements
front: Differentiate between 'pursuit movements' and 'saccades' in terms of target interaction and execution.
back:
• Pursuit: Smooth, slow tracking requiring a moving object; involves automatic computational tracking
• Saccades: Rapid, jerky jumps between fixed points; occurs even without moving targets
• Pursuit is more complex/subconscious than simple jumping

category: Describe the muscular and neural control of eye movements
front: Identify the nerve and action associated with the 'Superior Oblique' muscle.
back:
• Trochlear nerve (Cranial Nerve IV)
• Rotates eye medially (intorsion) and moves it downward (depression)
• Only muscle innervated by CN IV

category: Illustrate the abnormalities of field of vision
front: In clinical perimetry, the visual area perceived to the lateral side is known as the [___] field, while the area perceived medially is the [___] field.
back:
double-quoted as valid strings. Do not generate any comments inside the json block. Do not generate any control token (such as \n and \t) at any places. If a user requests multiple JSON, always return a single parseable JSON array. Do not include any extra text outside of the JSON string.

When producing JSON you must follow the schema provided in the context. 
* Temporal field.
* Nasal field.

category: Illustrate the abnormalities of field of vision
front: A 65-year-old male with chronic glaucoma shows progressive field loss. Explain the pathophysiology regarding the optic disc in this condition.
back:
* High intraocular pressure compresses axons at the optic disc.
* This blocks axonal flow of cytoplasm from retinal neuronal cell bodies.
* Results in fiber death and lack of nutrition.

category: Illustrate the abnormalities of field of vision
front: Explain the role of the 'voluntary fixation' mechanism versus the 'involuntary fixation' mechanism in directing visual gaze.
back:
* Voluntary: Controlled by premotor frontal fields; allows moving eyes to find an object.
* Involuntary: Controlled by secondary occipital areas; locks eyes on an object once found.

category: Illustrate the abnormalities of field of vision
front: Contrast the functional representation of the retinal fovea with the peripheral retina within the primary visual cortex.
back:
* Fovea: Occupies a disproportionately large area (hundreds of times more representation).
* Peripheral: Occupies minimal area despite covering the majority of the retinal surface.

category: Illustrate the abnormalities of field of vision
front: Specify the precise coordinate and anatomical cause of the physiological blind spot on a perimetry chart.
back:
* Coordinate: Approximately 15 degrees lateral to the central point of vision.
* Cause: Anatomical lack of rods and cones at the optic disc.

category: Illustrate the abnormalities of field of vision
front: The brain suppresses the visual image during rapid, jumping eye movements called [___] that occur at a rate of 2 to 3 per second during reading.
back:
* Saccades (or Opticokinetic movements).
* Allows the eye to extract information at successive fixation sites without motion blur.

category: Illustrate the abnormalities of field of vision
front: A patient is tested with different pupillary apertures. Explain the clinical effect of miosis on the 'depth of focus' of the visual system.
back:
* Miosis (small pupil) increases depth of focus.
* It forces light rays to pass through the center of the lens.
* Minimizes blur circles if the retina is displaced.

category: Illustrate the abnormalities of field of vision
front: Describe the negative feedback mechanism involving 'flicks' that maintains foveal fixation despite slow eye drifting.
back:
* Drifting: Image moves toward the foveal edge.
* Flicking: A sudden reflex reaction triggered by the superior colliculi.
* Result: The image is snapped back to the foveal center.

category: Illustrate the abnormalities of field of vision
front: Contrast the diagnostic criteria for 'Simple cells' versus 'Complex cells' in the visual cortex analysis of borders.
back:
* Simple Cells: Require a specific line orientation at a fixed retinal position.
* Complex Cells: Respond to specific orientation even if the line is displaced laterally/vertically.

category: Illustrate the abnormalities of field of vision
front: Identify the three pairs of extraocular muscles and their primary axes of movement.
back:
* Medial/Lateral Recti: Side-to-side movements.
* Superior/Inferior Recti: Upward and downward movements.
* Obliques: Rotation of the eyeballs for upright visual fields.

category: Illustrate the abnormalities of field of vision
front: On a standard perimetry chart, the [___] field of vision is the largest, extending approximately 90 to 100 degrees from the central point.
back:
- Temporal field.
- This extensive range is possible because there are no anatomical obstructions (like the nose or brow) on the lateral side of the eye.

category: Illustrate the abnormalities of field of vision
front: A 60-year-old male with a history of hypertension presents with a sudden loss of the upper half of the visual field in his right eye. Identify the specific term for this defect.
back:
- Altitudinal Hemianopia.
- It is frequently caused by vascular events such as Ischemic Optic Neuropathy or branch retinal artery occlusion.

category: Illustrate the abnormalities of field of vision
front: Explain the pathophysiological reason why peripheral vision is typically compromised before central vision in chronic open-angle glaucoma.
back:
- Axons from the peripheral retina are located at the periphery of the optic nerve head.
- These fibers are more susceptible to initial mechanical compression and ischemia at the optic disc rim.

category: Illustrate the abnormalities of field of vision
front: Distinguish between a 'Positive Scotoma' and a 'Negative Scotoma' based on the patient's subjective perception of the visual defect.
back:
- Positive Scotoma: Perceived by the patient as a dark spot or shadow (often due to retinal disease).
- Negative Scotoma: Not perceived by the patient; only detectable via perimetry.

category: Illustrate the abnormalities of field of vision
front: Identify the visual field abnormality resulting from an internal carotid artery aneurysm compressing the lateral, non-decussating fibers of the optic chiasm.
back:
- Nasal Hemianopia.
- This occurs because the temporal retinal fibers (which perceive the nasal field) on the side of the lesion are selectively damaged.

category: Illustrate the abnormalities of field of vision
front: The vertical meridian, which anatomically segregates the nasal and temporal halves of the retina, passes through the [___].
back:
- Fovea (Macula).
- Fibers nasal to this line decussate at the chiasm, while fibers temporal to it remain ipsilateral.

category: Illustrate the abnormalities of field of vision
front: A patient presents with a central scotoma in the left eye and a superior temporal field defect in the right eye. Identify the anatomical site of the lesion.
back:
- Left optic nerve at its junction with the optic chiasm.
- This is known as 'Anterior Junction Syndrome' (involving Wilbrand's knee).

category: Illustrate the abnormalities of field of vision
front: Describe the mechanism of 'congruity' in homonymous hemianopia and its value in localizing a lesion within the visual pathway.
back:
- Congruity refers to how identical the defects are in both eyes.
- Highly congruous defects suggest an occipital cortex lesion; incongruous (dissimilar) defects suggest an optic tract lesion.

category: Illustrate the abnormalities of field of vision
front: Contrast 'Kinetic Perimetry' with 'Static Perimetry' in the assessment of visual field abnormalities.
back:
- Kinetic: A moving light of fixed intensity is brought from the periphery until seen.
- Static: Stationary lights of varying intensities are flashed to determine the threshold at specific points.

category: Illustrate the abnormalities of field of vision
front: Define the term 'Hemianopsia' and state the primary difference between homonymous and heteronymous types.
back:
- Hemianopsia: Blindness in one-half of the visual field.
- Homonymous: Same side (both right or both left).
- Heteronymous: Opposite sides (e.g., both temporal or both nasal).

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: Strabismus, colloquially known as squint, is defined as the lack of [___] of the eyes in one or more of the visual coordinates.
back: Fusion. (1) Occurs in horizontal, vertical, or rotational axes. (2) Results in misaligned visual axes. (3) Prevents normal binocular single vision.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: A child presents with 'cross-eye' where the visual axes intersect in front of the patient. Identify the specific clinical term for this horizontal misalignment.
back: Esotropia. (1) A form of horizontal strabismus. (2) Characterized by inward deviation. (3) Often results in cortical suppression of the deviating eye to prevent diplopia.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: Explain the sensory mechanism used by the brain to mitigate double vision (diplopia) in a patient with chronic, uncorrected strabismus.
back: Cortical Suppression. (1) The brain inhibits the visual signal from the non-fixating eye. (2) Prevents confusion from non-corresponding retinal points. (3) Leads to loss of visual acuity (amblyopia).

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: Contrast the mechanical failure in Torsional strabismus with that of Horizontal strabismus regarding the muscle groups involved.
back: Mechanical Contrast. (1) Torsional: Involves Superior and Inferior Obliques (rotational failure). (2) Horizontal: Involves Medial and Lateral Recti (side-to-side failure). (3) Torsional affects visual field uprightness.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: Identify the three primary visual coordinates in which fusion may fail, resulting in different clinical presentations of strabismus.
back: Visual Coordinates. (1) Horizontal (lateral/medial deviation). (2) Vertical (upward/downward deviation). (3) Rotational (torsional deviation).

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: In the classification of vertical strabismus, the downward deviation of one eye relative to the fixating eye is specifically termed [___].
back: Hypotropia. (1) Subtype of vertical strabismus. (2) Involves dysfunction of the superior/inferior recti. (3) Contrast with Hypertropia (upward deviation).

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: An adult patient develops sudden-onset exotropia. Describe the likely mechanical cause and the effect on the patient's depth perception.
back: Exotropia Mechanism. (1) Cause: Weakness of the Medial Rectus or CN III palsy. (2) Deviation: Outward/lateral. (3) Effect: Loss of stereopsis due to lack of retinal registration.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: Describe the physiological process of 'interference excitation' in the visual cortex when eyes are not precisely 'in register'.
back: Cortical Adjustment. (1) Occurs when images on corresponding retinal points do not match. (2) Specific neurons fire to signal non-registration. (3) Signals trigger oculomotor apparatus to rotate/converge eyes for fusion.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: Distinguish between 'Concomitant' and 'Paralytic' strabismus based on the consistency of the deviation angle across different gazes.
back: Deviation Consistency. (1) Concomitant: Constant angle of deviation in all directions. (2) Paralytic: Angle varies with gaze direction due to specific nerve/muscle palsy. (3) Paralytic often causes acute diplopia.

category: Define and enlist the types of Strabismus
front: List the three pairs of extraocular muscles that must be precisely coordinated by the brainstem to prevent strabismus.
back: Extraocular Pairs. (1) Medial and Lateral Recti. (2) Superior and Inferior Recti. (3) Superior and Inferior Obliques.
